title: Heller and McDonald
short: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), 5 to 4, held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, struck down a handgun ban and said some longstanding regulations remain lawful; McDonald v. Chicago (2010) incorporated the right against the states.
trouble: Students state the militia clause's role as settled before Heller. The majority read the prefatory clause as announcing a purpose; Justice Stevens's dissent read the right as tied to militia service. Present both readings.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

For most of the 1900s the Court said little about the Second Amendment. In United States v. Miller (1939) it upheld a federal tax on short-barreled shotguns because no evidence showed such a weapon related to a well regulated militia. Then, in 2008, the Court decided its first full case on the amendment's meaning. You met it in Civics: the Second Amendment.

doc.title: The Second Amendment
paras: A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.

marks.text: A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State
marks.note: The prefatory clause: it announces a purpose.

marks.text: the right of the people to keep and bear Arms
marks.note: The operative clause: Heller read it as an individual right.

opts.facts: The District of Columbia banned handguns in the home and required other firearms at home to be kept unloaded and disassembled or trigger-locked. Dick Heller, a special police officer who carried a handgun on duty, was refused a license to keep one at home.
opts.reasoning: Justice Scalia's majority read the operative clause as protecting an individual right to keep and bear arms, especially for self-defense in the home, and the prefatory clause as announcing a purpose without limiting the right. The handgun ban failed under any standard. The Court added that "longstanding prohibitions" (such as on possession by felons and the mentally ill, carrying in sensitive places like schools and government buildings, and conditions on commercial sale) were "presumptively lawful," and that the right covers weapons in common use, not "dangerous and unusual" ones.
opts.dissent: Justice Stevens (joined by three) read the amendment as protecting the right to have arms in connection with service in a state militia, citing its text and the founding debates. Justice Breyer (joined by three) argued that even an individual right should yield to reasonable regulation under interest balancing.

blocks.html: Heller is a leading example of the debate between interpretive methods you met in Con Law I: originalism. Both main opinions argued from founding-era history; they read it differently. Scholars remain divided, and both readings are presented here as their advocates present them. Two years later, McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010) held 5 to 4 that the right applies to states and cities: a plurality (Justice Alito) used the Due Process Clause, finding the right fundamental and deeply rooted, and Justice Thomas, concurring, used the Privileges or Immunities Clause (see incorporation). Chicago's handgun ban fell.

District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), 5 to 4: the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms; D.C.'s handgun ban fell; longstanding regulations remain presumptively lawful. McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010) incorporated the right against the states.

blocks.title: Two clauses
blocks.q: How did the Heller majority and Justice Stevens's dissent read "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State"?
steps: Majority: a prefatory clause announcing a purpose; it does not limit the operative clause's individual right.
Stevens: the clause shows the right was tied to militia service.
blocks.a: Majority: a statement of purpose; Stevens: a limit tying the right to the militia.

blocks.title: A state law after McDonald
blocks.q: In 2011 a city bans keeping handguns in the home. Can it argue the Second Amendment binds only the federal government?
steps: That was true before 2010 (the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government under Barron, and the Court had not incorporated this right).
McDonald v. Chicago (2010) incorporated it against states and cities.
Heller held a home handgun ban unconstitutional.
blocks.a: No; after McDonald, the city's ban is unconstitutional under Heller.

blocks.html: Stating the militia clause's role as settled before Heller. Before 2008 lower courts mostly followed a militia-related reading, but the Supreme Court had not squarely decided the question. In Heller, the majority read the prefatory clause as announcing a purpose; Justice Stevens's dissent read the right as tied to militia service. Present both readings.
